summary: German has no single plural ending: there are five patterns, and the vowel often takes an umlaut (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü). -e: der Tisch – die Tische, der Stuhl – die Stühle. -er (with umlaut where possible): das Kind – die Kinder, das Buch – die Bücher. -(e)n: die Frau – die Frauen, die Lampe – die Lampen, die Lehrerin – die Lehrerinnen. -s (mostly loanwords and words ending in a vowel): das Handy – die Handys, das Baby – die Babys. No ending (often nouns in -er, -el, -chen): das Zimmer – die Zimmer, der Lehrer – die Lehrer, and with umlaut only: die Mutter – die Mütter, der Bruder – die Brüder. Learn every noun with its article and plural, as a dictionary gives it (der Stuhl, -e). The plural article is always die (dieser → diese, mein → meine), the indefinite article has no plural (ein Buch → Bücher), and in the dative plural the noun adds -n unless it already ends in -n or -s: den Kindern, but den Frauen, den Handys.

blocks.title: The dative plural adds -n
blocks.text: die Kinder → mit den Kindern, die Männer → den Männern, die Brüder → den Brüdern. No extra -n when the plural already ends in -n or -s: den Frauen, den Lampen, den Handys, den Omas.

blocks.title: Rules of thumb (not laws)
blocks.text: Feminine → usually -(e)n (and -in → -innen). Nouns in -chen, -lein, and masculine/neuter nouns in -er, -el, -en → no ending. Loanwords (das Handy, das Baby, der Cousin) and nouns ending in a vowel other than -e → -s. One-syllable masculines → often -e, often with umlaut. One-syllable neuters → often -er with umlaut.

blocks.title: Plural only
blocks.text: die Leute (people), die Eltern (parents), die Großeltern (grandparents) have no singular: one person = eine Person, one parent = ein Elternteil.

askYourself: Which plural did I learn with this noun (der Stuhl, -e → die Stühle)?
Is it feminine? Then -(e)n is very likely; a female noun in -in takes -innen.
Does it end in -er, -el, -en or -chen (masculine or neuter)? Then no ending – maybe an umlaut (Mütter, Väter, Brüder).
Is it a loanword or does it end in a vowel (Handy, Baby, Opa)? Then often -s.
Is it a one-syllable neuter (Kind, Buch, Haus)? Then often -er with umlaut.
Is it dative plural? Add -n unless the plural already ends in -n or -s.
steps: Use die (nominative/accusative), den (dative) or der (genitive); no article for “some”.

traps: Umlaut only: die Mutter – die Mütter, der Vater – die Väter, der Bruder – die Brüder, die Tochter – die Töchter (die Muttern are nuts for bolts!).
Same form in the singular and plural: das Zimmer – die Zimmer, der Lehrer – die Lehrer, das Mädchen – die Mädchen, der Enkel – die Enkel.
Dative plural adds -n: den Kindern, den Männern – but not after -n or -s: den Frauen, den Handys.
Loanwords: das Baby – die Babys (not *Babies), der Cousin – die Cousins.
Weak masculines take -n everywhere: der Junge – die Jungen, der Neffe – die Neffen.
ein has no plural: ein Buch – Bücher (no article).
Leute, Eltern and Großeltern have no singular.

quiz.why: Masculine in -er: no ending (Lehrern is the dative plural).
Umlaut only; Muttern are nuts for bolts.

quiz.q: Which article goes with every plural noun?
quiz.why: die Stühle, die Lampen, die Bücher – one plural article for all three genders.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has a dual (two) and “broken” plurals made inside the word (kitāb → kutub) – a bigger version of German Buch → Bücher.
Hebrew plurals end mostly in -im (masculine) and -ot (feminine), with exceptions; the vowels inside the word often change too.
Chinese nouns do not change; numbers and measure words show the amount, 们 is added only for people.
After zwei and above the noun is plural: zwei Stühle, zehn Kinder.

notes.text: Greek also has several plural endings by gender and declension (-οι, -ες, -α), but never changes the vowel inside the word; German often does: Buch → Bücher, Stuhl → Stühle.
Several endings (-ы, -и, -а) are familiar, but German adds umlaut (Buch → Bücher) and has no special forms after numbers: zwei Bücher, fünf Bücher.
Spanish adds -s / -es; German has five patterns, often with umlaut, so the plural is learned with each noun: der Stuhl, die Stühle.
English -s is one German pattern (Handys, Babys), and man – men, foot – feet show the same old vowel change as Mann – Männer; in German that change is everywhere: Buch – Bücher, Haus – Häuser.
In French the plural is mostly heard on the article (le / les); German shows it on the article (die) and usually on the noun too: der Tisch – die Tische.
Hindi plurals depend on gender and ending (laṛkā → laṛke, kitāb → kitābẽ), as German ones depend on gender and ending; German adds umlaut and five patterns.
Persian has one main plural, -hā (ketābhā), and keeps the noun singular after numbers; German has five patterns and always uses the plural after zwei.
Marathi plurals also depend on the noun’s gender and ending; German adds the vowel change (umlaut): Buch – Bücher.

Arabic broken plurals change the vowels inside the word (kitāb → kutub); German umlaut does something similar on a small scale (Buch → Bücher). German has no dual (kitābāni = zwei Bücher) and no singulative: “a tree” is ein Baum, not a form derived from the collective.
Hebrew plural -im / -ot is regular, and pairs and some time words take a dual (yomayim); German has five patterns and no dual: zwei Tage.
One plural suffix in Turkish (-ler / -lar); German has five patterns – learn the plural with each noun – and needs the plural after numbers too (zwei Bücher, iki kitap).
Japanese usually leaves number unmarked (hon = book or books); in German a plural noun must change: Buch – Bücher, Tisch – Tische.
Korean -deul is optional; the German plural is obligatory and has five patterns.
Finnish has one regular plural (-t, -i-: talot, taloissa); German has five patterns and the umlaut, learned with each noun.
Hungarian has one plural, -k with a linking vowel (házak), and uses the singular after numbers; German has five patterns and uses the plural after zwei.
Swahili makes the plural by changing the class prefix (kitabu → vitabu, mtu → watu); German changes the end of the word, often the vowel too (Buch → Bücher), and the article becomes die.
The plural is a different class prefix (omuntu → abantu, ekitabo → ebitabo); German changes the ending and often the vowel (Buch → Bücher) and uses die for every plural.
Chinese nouns do not change for number (们 only for people); every German plural noun changes, and must be learned: Tisch – Tische, Buch – Bücher.
Vietnamese marks plural with những / các before the noun if at all; German changes the noun itself (Buch – Bücher) and the article (die).
Inuktitut has singular, dual and plural endings (inuk, inuuk, inuit); German has no dual – two people are zwei Menschen, with the ordinary plural.
